parsed.summary: The second theorem asserts a nonzero, compactly supported, smooth, divergence-free, rapidly decaying u₀ on ℝ³ and a T* ∈ (0,1]. Its Euler solution is in an all-order L²-Sobolev class on [0,T*) with bounded energy, and closed-interval solutions in that class exist exactly for T < T*. The C¹ norms and vorticity time-integrals are finite on shorter intervals. At T* the limsup of ‖v‖_∞+‖∇v‖_∞ is ∞, ∫₀^{T*}‖curl v‖_∞ dt = ∞, and no global smooth finite-energy solution exists; the first theorem is this last clause alone. The main caveat: the paper's blow-up quantity is ‖∇u‖_{L∞}, but Lean's limsup clause uses the sum ‖u‖_∞+‖∇u‖_∞, which is literally weaker (equivalent only via an extra interpolation argument with bounded energy).

glossary.note: Every use is on smooth fields, so the fderiv junk value never arises.

glossary.plain: Additionally, ‖D^m u₀(x)‖ ≤ C_{m,K}(1+|x|)^{-K} for all m and all real K
glossary.note: Automatic for compactly supported smooth data.

glossary.plain: (u,p) are jointly C^∞ on ℝ³×[0,∞), solve ∂_t u+(u·∇)u=−∇p with ∇·u=0 for t≥0, and u(·,0)=u₀
glossary.note: The time derivative is one-sided at t=0.

glossary.plain: Additionally, u(t)∈L² for every t≥0 and sup_t ∫|u|² < E
L² class of f, or 0 if f ∉ L²
glossary.note: The fallback value is never reached, because MemLp is required wherever toL2 is used.

glossary.plain: v(·,t) is C^∞ with all D^m v(·,t)∈L², and t↦D^m v(·,t) is continuous into L² on I
glossary.standard_concept: C(I; H^∞) with smooth spatial representatives

glossary.plain: There is a velocity v in C(I;H^∞), div-free, with v(0)=u₀, and a strong L² time derivative w∈C(I;H^∞) at interior times, such that w+(v·∇)v=−∇p pointwise there; p is spatially differentiable at interior times
glossary.standard_concept: smooth H^∞ Euler solution on I
glossary.note: Pressure carries no decay or integrability condition. ∇p is nonetheless fixed by the equation, so this looks harmless.
The paper's blow-up quantity is ‖∇u‖_∞ alone; this definition adds ‖u‖_∞.

lean_claims.plain: There is a smooth, divergence-free u₀ with rapid decay of all derivatives such that no jointly smooth (u,p) on ℝ³×[0,∞) solves unforced Euler with u(0)=u₀, u(t)∈L² for all t, and uniformly bounded energy.

There exist u₀ (rapidly decaying, smooth, div-free, compactly supported, nonzero), T*∈(0,1], and (v,p) such that all of the following hold. (1) (v,p) is an H^∞ Euler solution on [0,T*) with bounded energy. (2) For every T>0, an H^∞ solution on [0,T] exists iff T<T*. (3) For every T<T*, sup_{[0,T]}(‖v‖_∞+‖∇v‖_∞)<∞ and ∫₀^T‖curl v‖_∞<∞. (4) limsup_{t↑T*}(‖v‖_∞+‖∇v‖_∞)=∞. (5) ∫₀^{T*}‖curl v‖_∞ dt=∞. (6) No global smooth finite-energy solution exists for u₀.

paper_claims.plain: There exists u₀∈C_c^∞(ℝ³;ℝ³), divergence-free, with 0<T*(u₀)<∞, whose smooth Euler solution satisfies limsup_{t↑T*}‖∇u(t)‖_{L∞}=∞ and ∫₀^{T*}‖curl u(t)‖_{L∞}dt=∞.

coverage.why: It is stronger in several respects: T*≤1, u₀≠0, explicit maximality characterization, local bounds, and a global nonexistence clause. It is literally weaker in the blow-up clause, which uses ‖u‖_∞+‖∇u‖_∞ instead of ‖∇u‖_∞.
This is the global-nonexistence consequence (Navier–Stokes-Millennium-style breakdown at ν=0), not the quantitative blow-up statement. Global nonexistence in this class is not stated in the excerpt.

flags.explanation: lintegral of a possibly non-measurable function is a lower integral. The '=⊤' claim is therefore at least as strong as intended, and the '<⊤' local claim may be weaker than an outer-integral reading. t↦‖curl v(t)‖_∞ is lower semicontinuous here, so this is likely harmless.
